titre: Japan's Jury Is Suspended in 1943 by a Twelve-Character Sentence
accroche: In 1943, a law whose main provision is twelve characters long suspends Japan's 1928 jury, with resumption planned after the war.
contenu_vulgarise:
On April 18, 1923, Japan promulgates Law No. 50, a jury law that brings citizens into the judging of criminal cases. The text provides for five years of preparation before it takes effect: the first jury trials are held starting October 1, 1928.

The system borrows from the Western model without copying it. Twelve jurors, drawn by lot from a list of men aged thirty or older, paying a minimum of direct tax and able to read and write, answer by majority the question of whether the alleged facts are established; the court then applies the law. Two categories of trials give access to it: the “obligatory jury,” for crimes punishable by death or life imprisonment, which the accused may refuse, and the “jury on request,” for sentences of more than three years, at the accused's request.

## A Jury the Judge Can Dismiss

Here the system departs most sharply from its model: the court is not bound by the jury's answer. If it judges the answer poorly founded, it may reject it and convene a second jury to retry the case, a procedure called jury renewal. Another major difference: a defendant found guilty by a jury loses the right to appeal the judgment on the facts, while a defendant tried by a judge alone keeps it. Requesting a jury thus means trading one procedural guarantee for another.

Defendants rarely take that gamble. In 1928, 31 jury trials are held; the following year, 143, a peak never reached again. The number then declines each year, to just two trials in 1942, for a total of 484 trials in fifteen years of existence.

## A Suspension Never Lifted

Promulgated on March 31, 1943 and published in the Official Gazette on April 1, in the middle of the Pacific War, Law No. 88 suspends the jury: its main provision is twelve characters long, 陪審法ハ其ノ施行ヲ停止ス, “the application of the Jury Act is suspended.” The Ministry of Justice dates the suspension to April 1, 1943. The text of the law states no reason; according to Japanese Wikipedia, as the war intensifies, municipalities overwhelmed by conscription duties struggle to draw up lists of jurors and ask for the system to be suspended. An additional clause provides for the law's resumption after the war ends, each article taking effect again on a date set by imperial ordinance.

The war ends in 1945. No such imperial ordinance is ever issued. Japan reintroduces citizens into its criminal trials in 2009, with a system of lay judges (saiban-in) built on different foundations; the 1943 law is not repealed for all that, and no resumption date for the 1928 jury has ever been set by ordinance. A suspension meant to last the length of a war ended up lasting longer than the war itself.

carte.punch: Twelve characters suspended Japan's jury in 1943; the planned resumption was never dated.
carte.idee: In 1928, Japan establishes a popular jury following a 1923 law. In 1943, a law whose main provision is twelve characters long suspends it and provides for its resumption after the war, by imperial ordinance. The war ends in 1945: that ordinance was never issued.

quiz.question: What distinguished the 1928 Japanese jury from an English-style jury?
choix: The jury had only six members instead of twelve
Only women over thirty could sit on it
The verdict had to be unanimous among the twelve jurors
The judge could reject the verdict and convene a new jury
quiz.explication: The 1928 Japanese jury did have twelve members, voted by majority rather than unanimity, and was open only to men; its real singularity is that the judge was not bound by its verdict and could convene a renewal jury if he judged it poorly founded.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Japanese jurors have to meet to be drawn by lot, once the law took effect in 1928?
choix: Be men aged thirty or older, pay a minimum of direct tax, and be able to read and write
Be men or women aged twenty-five or older, with no income requirement
Belong to a legal profession recognized by the Ministry of Justice
Have lived for at least ten years in the prefecture where the trial was held
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that jurors were drawn by lot from men aged thirty or older, paying a minimum of direct tax and able to read and write.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did a defendant give up by opting for a jury trial rather than a trial by a judge alone?
choix: The right to be assisted by a lawyer throughout the trial
The right to know in advance the identity of the jurors drawn by lot
The right to appeal the judgment on the facts in the event of a guilty verdict
The right to request the removal of a juror for conflict of interest
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A defendant found guilty by a jury lost the right to appeal the judgment on the facts, a right a defendant tried by a judge alone kept: requesting a jury traded one guarantee for another.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the additional clause of the 1943 suspension law, what was the Japanese state to do once the war ended?
choix: Resume the jury automatically upon signing the armistice, without formality
Set a resumption date for the jury by imperial ordinance, which was never done
Hold a national referendum to decide whether to keep the jury
Transfer the jury's powers to the newly created Supreme Court of Japan
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The additional clause provided for the law's resumption after the war, each article taking effect again on a date set by imperial ordinance; Japanese Wikipedia notes that the law was never put back into force.
